analysis.one_liner: Creates a national paid family and medical leave insurance program funded by a small payroll tax.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or any action after being referred to the Senate Finance Committee in February 2019, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021, with 36 Senate cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAMILY Act would have created a federal insurance program, run through the Social Security Administration, paying workers up to 60 days of partial wages when they need time off for a new child, their own serious illness, or the serious illness of a family member. It would be funded by a new payroll tax of 0.2% on both employees and employers (0.4% for the self-employed). Benefits would replace roughly two-thirds of pay, between $580 and $4,000 per month. The bill also made it illegal for an employer to fire or punish a worker for using the benefit.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who need paid time off to have or adopt a child, recover from their own serious health condition, or care for a child, spouse, parent, or domestic partner with a serious health condition. Only 17% of civilian workers had employer-paid family leave, and it reached just 5% of people in the lowest-paying jobs, so the bill's largest gains would go to workers least likely to have any coverage today.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers without paid leave, especially low-wage workers

how_it_helps.text: Every eligible worker could receive up to 60 caregiving days of benefits within a 365-day benefit period, replacing part of their usual wages — the monthly amount is roughly one-eighteenth of their highest recent year's earnings, between a $580 minimum and a $4,000 maximum.

Coverage reaches reasons beyond childbirth: a worker's own serious health condition, care for a child, spouse, parent, or domestic partner, care for an injured servicemember, and military deployment emergencies.

The bill makes it unlawful for an employer to fire or discriminate against a worker for applying for or receiving benefits, and lets workers sue for lost wages, double damages, reinstatement, and attorney's fees.
The bill's own findings cite evidence that paid leave keeps workers attached to jobs and that California's program reduced elder nursing home use and improved child health and breastfeeding rates.

analysis.who_pays: Employees and employers each pay a new 0.2% payroll tax on wages (0.4% combined for self-employed income) into a dedicated trust fund — about $100 per year for a worker earning $50,000, with the employer paying a matching $100. Self-employed people pay both halves.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers and workers, via a 0.2% payroll tax each

drawbacks.text: It is a new mandatory tax on every dollar of wages up to Social Security's taxable cap, falling on workers and employers alike, including businesses and workers who never take leave.

Benefits are modest and delayed: there is a waiting period of up to five days with no pay, the benefit replaces only a share of wages, capped at $4,000 a month, and claims could not be filed until 18 months after enactment.

The strongest good-faith objection is cost and design: a permanent new payroll tax and a new federal entitlement administered by the Social Security Administration, with critics typically arguing employers would offset the tax through lower wages and that state programs already running in California, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, and elsewhere would need coordination rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers facing a birth, adoption, or serious illness, the benefit is substantial — paid time they currently lose wages or jobs to take — paid for by a small, broadly shared tax (roughly $200 per year split between a $50,000 worker and their employer). The waiting period and wage caps keep the program from being generous, but the design mirrors state programs that have operated for years. The main honest objection is adding another permanent payroll tax rather than the program's structure.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in February 2019 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the FAMILY Act on February 12, 2019, with 34 Democratic senators and 2 independents as original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced.
That referral was the last action ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote appears in the bill's action history before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, and the bill's findings cite polling that more than eight in ten voters across party lines supported a national paid leave program.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off because the bill died: no new 0.2% payroll tax and no federal paid-leave mandate. Workers who needed paid family or medical leave gained nothing; the United States still has no national paid family leave program.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers avoiding a new payroll tax

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAMILY Act and organized 36 Senate cosponsors.

for.name: 36 Senate cosponsors (34 Democrats and 2 independents)
for.role: Original cosponsors including Sens. Sanders, Booker, Brown, Warren, Klobuchar, and Schumer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it the support of a large majority of the Senate's Democratic and independent members but no Republicans.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the entire two-year Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Controlled the Senate floor agenda in the 116th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; no Republican cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: All 36 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican senator signed on, and the bill received no floor action in a Senate controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: Employers would pay a new 0.2% payroll tax on wages and face an anti-retaliation mandate with double damages for punishing workers who take leave. The bill's findings report that most employers in state programs described neutral or positive effects, but the industry's interest in stopping the bill ran against workers' access to paid leave.
They would pay a 0.4% tax on self-employment income but gain access to leave benefits they currently cannot get from any employer.
